note: Per-match tactical breakdowns. Fields under `grounded` come from FotMob's match data and are never written by the LLM. Fields under `explained` are model commentary constrained to that data. `conceptsTaught` drives the lesson curriculum so it ramps instead of repeating.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal went to Villa Park, kept the ball for most of the afternoon and won 1-0. Neither side created much for long stretches — both teams had seven shots — but Arsenal's chances were the better ones, and Bukayo Saka scored on 59 minutes from a Riccardo Calafiori assist. Villa never once forced David Raya into a save.
explained.opponentPlan: Unai Emery matched Arsenal's 4-2-3-1, which is a way of saying every Arsenal player had a natural opponent and Villa were content to let Arsenal have the ball rather than chase it. The numbers back that up: Villa made 20 tackles to Arsenal's 13, but only three interceptions and 147 passes in the opposition half against Arsenal's 238. That is the profile of a team defending in its own territory and engaging late, once Arsenal had already carried the ball forward, rather than trying to win it back early. Arsenal answered it by simply refusing to force the issue — 61% possession, patient circulation, and 21 touches in the Villa box, which is how you eventually prise open a side that is well organised but not aggressive.
explained.keyMoment: The 59th minute: Calafiori to Saka for the only goal of the game. It matters not just because it was the winner but because of who supplied it — the left-sided defender arriving as a passer in the final third is exactly the by-product of Arsenal's in-possession shape, and it broke a match in which both teams had otherwise been trading harmless shots. From there Villa had to come out, and the shot-on-target column still finished 2-0 to Arsenal.
explained.nerdCorner: The interesting number is xGOT: Arsenal 0.8, Villa 0.0. xG measures the chance at the moment of the shot; xGOT measures it again once the ball is struck, and only counts shots on target. Villa's 0.0 means all seven of their attempts either missed or were blocked before they became a goalkeeper's problem — 0.33 xG of chances converted into precisely nothing that tested Raya. Meanwhile Arsenal's 1.04 xG shrank to 0.8 on target and yielded exactly one goal, which is the honest reading of the afternoon: this was a controlled 1-0, not a smash-and-grab, but it was also a match where Arsenal's control (61% possession, 238 passes in the opposition half) bought only two big chances. Against a manager who is happy to sit and match your shape, volume of possession is the cheap part; the expensive part is manufacturing that one extra man, and Arsenal did it once, in the 59th minute, through a defender.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper Arsenal lined up 4-2-3-1, but a back four rarely stays a back four when this side has the ball. One full-back — with Calafiori and Ben White either side, it is usually the left one — steps inside or forward, which leaves three defenders across the back, two holders like Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly in front of them, and five attackers spread across the width of the pitch. Without the ball those players walk back into two banks of four with the striker and the number ten leading the line, because a flat block is far easier to hold together than a lopsided attacking shape.

lesson.explain: An overload is simply getting more of your players into one area of the pitch than the opponent has defenders there. When both teams line up 4-2-3-1, every Arsenal player starts with a Villa player near him — so Arsenal have to manufacture an extra body somewhere, and the usual way is a full-back like Calafiori pushing high on one side so that the winger, the number ten and the full-back are three against two. That is how a defender ends up assisting a goal in the 59th minute rather than defending one. It is also why Arsenal could rack up 238 passes in the opposition half and 21 touches in the Villa box: you keep shifting the ball until one side of the pitch has a spare man, then attack that side.
lesson.spotIt: When Arsenal build down one flank, count the shirts in that corner of the screen — the moment Arsenal have three players there against two defenders, that is the overload, and the pass into the box is usually two touches away.

statTranslations.stat: Shots on target: Arsenal 2 | Aston Villa 0
statTranslations.plain: Villa had seven attempts and not one of them was on target — Raya made zero saves, so this was a clean sheet earned by the defensive shape rather than by the goalkeeper.
Equal shot counts (7-7) hide the truth: Arsenal created two genuinely presentable openings and Villa created none.
Based on the quality of the openings, an average team would score about one from Arsenal's chances and about a third of a goal from Villa's — so 1-0 is roughly the fair result.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in opposition half: Arsenal 238 | Aston Villa 147
statTranslations.plain: Arsenal spent far more of the game playing football in Villa's territory, which is where 61% possession actually becomes dangerous rather than decorative.

statTranslations.stat: Tackles: Arsenal 13 | Aston Villa 20, Interceptions: Arsenal 9 | Aston Villa 3
statTranslations.plain: Villa were reacting — lunging in once Arsenal had the ball under control — while Arsenal were reading passes before they arrived and cutting them out.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal took control at home and never let go. Kai Havertz scored on 15 minutes from a Riccardo Calafiori pass, Bukayo Saka added a second on 23, and Martin Ødegaard made it three just after the break on 49 with Ben White setting him up. Coventry managed only four shots all match and Arsenal finished 3-0 winners.
explained.opponentPlan: Frank Lampard set Coventry up in a matching 4-3-3, which on paper gives you a man for every Arsenal man, but the possession split of 64% to 36% tells you they spent most of the afternoon defending rather than contesting. Their 9 interceptions against Arsenal's 5 is the signature of a team sitting in their own shape and reading passes rather than chasing the ball — they were trying to clog the space in front of their back four and force Arsenal wide. Arsenal's answer was volume and width: 8 corners, 335 passes in the opposition half and 36 touches in the Coventry box, working the ball around the block until something opened. Coventry's own attacking output collapsed to 4 shots and 3 touches in the Arsenal box, so whatever counter-attacking plan existed never got going.
explained.keyMoment: The eight minutes between Havertz's goal on 15 and Saka's on 23. Coventry's 4-3-3 was built to stay compact and matched up, and a shape like that can survive a long time at 0-0 — but two goals inside that window forced them to come out of it. Ødegaard's third on 49, assisted by Ben White from the right, was the confirmation: a full-back arriving in an advanced position to set up a goal is the kind of chance a team only concedes once its defensive shape has been pulled apart.
explained.nerdCorner: Big chances finished level at 1 apiece, which is the single most misleading line in the data set — and also the most instructive. Arsenal scored three goals from a match in which they created, by that metric, exactly as many gilt-edged openings as the team that lost 3-0. The reconciliation is in the gap between xG 1.88 and xGOT 2.44: Arsenal generated a large volume of decent-but-not-outstanding looks (20 shots, 10 of them inside the box) and then converted at a rate above what those looks were worth. Only 6 of 20 shots hit the target, so this was not a night of relentless accuracy — it was a night where the six that did land were struck extremely well. The sustainable part of the performance is the territory: 36 box touches, 335 passes in the opposition half, 8 corners. The unsustainable part is the 0.56 of extra value between xG and xGOT. Repeat the first set of numbers weekly and the wins keep coming; bank on the second set and you will be disappointed at some point.

shape.plainEnglish: On paper both sides lined up 4-3-3, but a formation is only the kick-off photo. With the ball, an Arteta side of this type usually slides one full-back — with Ben White and Calafiori as the pair, it is typically Calafiori stepping in from the left — so the back four becomes a back three plus an extra body in midfield, and five attackers stretch across the last line. Without the ball those players fold back the other way: the wide forwards drop into a bank of four and Arsenal defend as a 4-4-2 instead.

lesson.explain: Both teams were recorded as 4-3-3, and yet the match was nothing like a mirror image — because the number you see on the team sheet only describes the moment before kick-off. A side like this one typically becomes something closer to a 3-2-5 with the ball, with a full-back tucking inside so there are more passers in midfield and five bodies stretched across the opponent's last line, and then folds back into a 4-4-2 bank when the ball is lost. That is why Arsenal could produce 36 touches in the Coventry box while Coventry managed 3: the shapes were identical on paper and completely different in practice. Ben White assisting Ødegaard's goal on 49 is exactly what that looks like — a defender by formation, an attacker by shape.
lesson.spotIt: At the next goal kick, find Arsenal's two full-backs and watch where they are ten seconds later — if one has stepped inside next to Declan Rice instead of staying wide, you have just watched a back four turn into a back three.

statTranslations.plain: Arsenal had the ball roughly two-thirds of the match, so almost everything that happened was Arsenal attacking a set defence rather than an open, end-to-end game.
This is the cleanest measure of territory in the whole list — Arsenal got into the dangerous area twelve times more often than Coventry did.
Arsenal weren't just shooting a lot, they were shooting from good places; Coventry got one shot from inside the box all match.
Arsenal's chances were worth about 1.88 goals on average, but the shots that actually hit the target were worth 2.44 — meaning the finishing and shot placement beat the raw chance quality.
Coventry made nearly twice as many interceptions, which sounds good but usually just means one team is doing all the passing and the other is doing all the reading.

explained.whatHappened: Arsenal scored after 23 seconds and never trailed. What the scoreline hides is that City had more of the ball, more shots and more touches in Arsenal's box — Arsenal won by creating four clear chances to City's one and putting them away.

shape.plainEnglish: Arsenal started 4-3-3 and City 4-2-3-1, but neither held that shape for long. With the ball Arsenal's left-back steps inside, which turns the back four into a back three and pushes five players onto the last line. Without the ball — which was most of this match — Arsenal folded into two compact banks of four and let City pass in front of them.

explained.opponentPlan: Maresca's City did what they were set up to do: 59% of the ball and 310 passes in Arsenal's half, against Arsenal's 110 in theirs. They got 34 touches in the Arsenal box to Arsenal's 27. What they could not do was turn any of that into a clear opening — one big chance all afternoon, and an xGOT of 0.34 says the few shots they did work were struck straight at Raya.
explained.keyMoment: The first goal, 23 seconds in. Lewis-Skelly found Calafiori for a finish before City had touched the ball. That one moment set the terms for everything after it: Arsenal could sit deep and defend a lead, and City had to come out, which is exactly the game Arsenal wanted.

lesson.explain: This is the match to learn it from, because the stats look like Arsenal lost. City had 59% of the ball, 12 shots to 9, and 34 touches in the box to 27. Arsenal deliberately gave all of that away: they dropped into two banks of four, defended the space in front of their own goal rather than chasing the ball, and made 16 tackles and 10 interceptions doing it. A low block concedes territory on purpose and bets that the opponent will never get a clean look at goal. City managed one big chance. Arsenal managed four.
lesson.spotIt: Next match, when Arsenal are ahead and the opponent has the ball, stop watching the ball and look at the shape. Two flat rows of four, squeezed into the width of the penalty area, with nobody chasing out to press — that is the low block doing its job, and it is not the same thing as being under pressure.

statTranslations.plain: The number that actually explains a 3-0. Arsenal made four genuinely clear openings; City made one.
Arsenal's chances were worth about 2.2 goals and City's about 1.1 — a real edge, but much closer than 3-0 suggests.
Where the match was won. Arsenal struck their shots far better than the chances deserved; City struck theirs far worse, firing straight at Raya.
Arsenal had well under half the ball and were entirely content with that.

statTranslations.stat: Passes in the opposition half: 110 vs 310
statTranslations.plain: City spent almost three times as much of the match camped in Arsenal's territory — and still lost 3-0.

explained.nerdCorner: The xG-to-xGOT gap is the whole story and it cuts both ways. Arsenal turned 2.16 xG into 2.53 xGOT — their finishing beat the quality of the chances. City turned 1.12 into 0.34, meaning their shooting was dreadful relative to the openings. That combined swing is worth roughly two and a half goals of finishing, and it is the least repeatable thing in football: expect both numbers to drift back toward their xG over a season. The more durable read is the big-chance count. Conceding 59% possession and 310 opposition-half passes while allowing exactly one clear sight of goal is a defensive structure working precisely as designed, and that part does repeat.
